title: A support desk where a document edited five minutes ago must be findable
body:
> **Casebook thread.** A reconstructed conversation, written for teaching. The people in it
> are illustrative; **every number is real** and reproducible from the notebook cited below.
> Replies are welcome — if you hit this yourself, add your numbers.

### The constraints

- **Freshness:** an agent edits a KB article mid-call. It must be retrievable within **60 seconds**
- **Corpus:** 180k articles, ~400 edits/day, bursty — a product incident causes 200 edits in an hour
- **Latency:** 800ms p95 end to end
- **Team:** two engineers, no dedicated infra

### The tension

Everything about a fresh index is cheap except the **embedding**. A 60-second SLA on edits means
re-embedding on the write path, and the encoder is the slowest thing in the system.

### Proposed design

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    E["article edited"] --> Q["write queue"]
    Q --> C["re-chunk, stable ids"]
    C --> H{"content hash changed?"}
    H -->|no| S["skip — no re-embed"]
    H -->|yes| B["embed, 2s batch window"]
    B --> U["upsert into live version"]
    U --> L["lexical index updated synchronously"]
```

**Key choices:**

1. **Lexical updates synchronously, dense asynchronously.** BM25 insert is microseconds; the
   article is findable by its own words immediately, semantically within ~10s.
2. **Content-hash gate before embedding.** Most "edits" are metadata or whitespace. Stable chunk
   ids make this free.
3. **Upsert into the live version rather than building a new one.** Freshness beats the safety of
   version aliasing here, and I am not comfortable about it.

### What I am least sure about

Point 3. Every other design in this repository says *build alongside, then swap the alias*. A
60-second SLA does not permit that. Am I trading away the wrong thing?

comments.body:
> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

Point 3 is the right trade and you are right to be uncomfortable, but not for the reason you think.

Upserting into the live version is fine for **content** edits. It is not fine for **encoder**
changes, and the design does not distinguish them. Same operation, completely different blast
radius: a content edit touches one chunk; an encoder change invalidates every vector in the index
and there is nothing to compare against because you overwrote it.

Add one guard: **the write path refuses any upsert whose `embedder_tag` differs from the live
version's.** Encoder changes go down the build-alongside-and-swap path; content edits go straight
in. One line, and it keeps the fast path fast without letting it eat the safe path.

Without it, a partially-completed migration leaves a mixed index that returns well-formed numbers
for vectors that mean nothing to each other, and **nothing errors**.

replies.body:
Accepted, and it is the change I would not have found. The two operations look identical at the API
and have completely different recovery stories.

Moving `mixed_version_check()` onto the write path, not only before an alias swap.

comments.body:
> **Dana** · reviewer · owns the eval harness

The design is sound. What is missing is what is missing from most freshness designs: **how do you
know the SLA is being met?**

"Retrievable within 60 seconds" is a claim about a distribution and nothing measures it. Before
this ships:

- **A canary write.** Every 5 minutes, write a document containing a unique nonce, then poll for
  it. Record time-to-findable for the lexical and dense legs **separately**
- **p50 and p99, not a mean.** The bursty case is exactly where a mean lies to you
- **Alert on queue depth, not on latency.** By the time time-to-findable degrades you are already
  outside the SLA; queue depth is the leading indicator

The canary is about twenty lines and it turns "we think it is fast" into a number somebody can be
woken up by.

replies.body:
> **Priya** · cohort peer

Adding to the canary: reporting the two legs separately is not just diagnostics, it is the
**client-facing sentence**.

If lexical is 200ms and dense is 12s, the honest statement is *"findable by its own words in under
a second, semantically within fifteen"* — far more useful to a support manager than one number
that averages two mechanisms with different guarantees.

Both in. The two-leg sentence is what I would actually put in front of the client and I would not
have written it without this.

comments.body:
Marking Dana's, because a freshness design with no freshness measurement is a promise, and this
thread turned it into a system.

| Critique | Verdict | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Write path must refuse encoder-tag mismatches | **Accepted** | `mixed_version_check()` on the write path |
| No measurement of the SLA | **Accepted** | Canary every 5 min, p50/p99, alert on queue depth |
| Report both legs separately | **Accepted** | And it becomes the client-facing sentence |

**Stands:** synchronous lexical, asynchronous dense, content-hash gate. Nobody challenged those and
they are the load-bearing parts.

**Open:** the 200-edits-in-an-hour burst. The queue absorbs it, but the dense leg falls behind
exactly when those articles are most needed. Shedding? Priority by article popularity? I have no
good answer and it deserves its own thread.
